title: Brazilian footballer falls in tunnel after scoring disallowed goal
text:
Brazilian footballer Jacy Maranhão was rushing to meet a sea of his supporters, ball in hand and jumping with joy, before he fell down a dark tunnel.

The Corbita defender had just put his club 2-0 up against Chapecoense in the first half of a game in the Brazilian Serie A.

But just as he found his footing again and dusted himself off from the fall, the referee halted the game.

On review, the Video Assistant Referee (VAR) found the 29-year-old's goal was offside.

Jacy managed to continue playing into the first few minutes of the second half before being substituted with an injury.

The incident was not the first time a footballer had fallen foul of the tunnel at the Estádio Major Antônio Couto Pereira.

Loading...

Almost a decade earlier, Cameroonian forward Diederrick Joel Tagueu-Tadjo ran to the same end of the pitch, jumping over the same advertising hoardings before falling into the now-infamous Corbita tunnel.

But unlike Jacy, his goal was not ruled out, and he managed to finish the game against São Paulo.

But according to Brazilian journalist Leonardo Mendes Jr, there was a striking similarity to the two incidents.

"There's one detail that makes it even more unbelievable," he posted on social media.

title: Chiefs sign premiership winger To'o away from Panthers
text:
Four-time premiership-winning winger Brian To'o has become the sixth player to sign with the PNG Chiefs for their inaugural NRL season in 2028.

The signing of the Penrith Panthers flyer, who has represented NSW in State of Origin and Samoa in Test matches, was announced by the Chiefs on Monday.

To'o has signed a three-year deal to join the Chiefs, with 2027 to be his final year with the Panthers.

Why Luai's move to PNG has changed everything Jarome Luai's decision to sign with Papua New Guinea is a showcase of the economic power behind the Chiefs and marks the start of the greatest rugby league gold rush since Super League.

"Brian is an exceptional rugby league player, but this signing is about much more than football," PNG Chiefs CEO Lorna McPherson said.

"The PNG Chiefs will be a club proudly built in Papua New Guinea but with a strong Pacific identity.

"Across our region, family, culture, community and rugby league are deeply connected, and Brian represents those values every time he takes the field.

"He is fiercely proud of his Samoan heritage, incredibly close to his family and understands what it means to represent something bigger than yourself.

"That is exactly the kind of person we want wearing the Chiefs jersey."

To'o has been a key component of the Penrith Panthers dynasty, which won four consecutive premierships from 2021–2024, were grand finalists in 2020 and made last year's preliminary final.

The Panthers are on top of the NRL ladder in 2026, seeking a fifth title in six years.

To'o has played 151 matches for the Panthers since making his debut in 2019, scoring 99 tries to date.

He has played 17 Origins for the Blues, and 11 Tests for Samoa.

"Brian is an exceptional player, but he's an even better person. He's a great teammate, a devoted family man and someone who brings so much energy and positivity to our club every day," Penrith coach Ivan Cleary said.

"He's been a huge part of what we've built here and we're looking forward to sharing one more season with him before he begins his next chapter."

The Chiefs have now signed six players to its maiden roster, but have already secured key talent.

Former Penrith five-eighth Jarome Luai, who won four premierships with To'o, was the club's marquee signing earlier this year.

Alex Johnston, the all-time leading try scorer in Australian premiership rugby league, was a key outside back signed along with NSW Origin representative Zac Lomax.

Sydney Roosters utility Connor Watson and Englishman Matty Lees have also been signed.

title: Yeo learns fate on pec in seismic moment for Panthers
text:
Penrith's premiership charge has received a massive boost, with Isaah Yeo a chance to play again this year after avoiding surgery on his pectoral injury.

Yeo had been at risk of missing the rest of the NRL season after he left the field in Friday's loss to the Warriors, in what shaped as a major blow for the Panthers.

But Penrith medical staff confirmed on Monday the club's co-captain would not go under the knife following scans, and could begin rehabilitation in a bid to play again in 2026.

The news will also likely come as a relief to Australia coach Kevin Walters, with Yeo expected to again lead the Kangaroos at the World Cup if he avoids later surgery.

Former Panther Apisai Koroisau missed just one week with a pectoral injury early this year, as opposed to the 10 weeks usually out if surgery is required.

Penrith has made a habit of having players play through injury to be part of premiership wins throughout their dynasty.

Almost half of their squad were walking wounded through the first title of their four-peat in 2021, which the club compared to climbing Mount Everest.

Halves Jarome Luai and Nathan Cleary both played through persistent shoulder issues in 2023 and 2024 respectively, with both requiring surgery afterwards.

Had Yeo been sidelined, it would have been a monumental blow to the first-placed Panthers, given the role he plays in both attack and defence at lock.

Ex-Panther Spencer Leniu described Yeo as the "heartbeat" of Penrith's team over the weekend, declaring his injury would be a "massive loss" for the club.

Penrith faces Leniu's Sydney Roosters in a blockbuster top-of-the-table clash on Thursday night, which Yeo would not be expected to play in.

AAP

title: After decades of pleas, fallen miners from a historic mine will be memorialised
text:
After almost 30 years of advocacy, a multimillion dollar memorial honouring 151 fallen workers who died at a historic mine will be built in outback Queensland.

The $4.7 million Mount Isa Miners Memorial will be jointly funded by the state government, the mine's current owner Glencore, and the Mount Isa City Council.

Overlooking Mount Isa Mines, which sits directly across from the North West Queensland town, the landmark set to be erected at Frank Aston Hill is expected to be completed by late 2027.

Designs for a proposed miners' memorial were drafted in 2023 and paid for by the Mount Isa City Council. (Supplied)

Former Mount Isa resident Steve Trevor lost his brother Tony in a mining accident in 1995 and said he has spent decades waiting for a formal memorial site.

"The memories are still sharp in my mind," Mr Trevor said.

Operations at the Mount Isa underground copper mine officially ceased last year. (Supplied)

"[The memorial] will bring recognition of a life lost. What they gave to their community is the ultimate sacrifice.

" They didn't come home. There's only a few people who can understand what that feels like. "

Steve Trevor (left) and John Moran have been advocating for a miners memorial to be built in Mount Isa for decades. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

Mr Trevor said his brother's death was still a haunting memory.

"I remember I got my call about my brother's passing at midnight, and it was terrible not just for myself but my family, my mother, my father," he said.

"It means not just a lot to myself, but there's the 151 families as well."

Former local John Moran, who first called for a memorial in 1998, said it was a historic day for Mount Isa.

"[The fallen miners] were residents of Mount Isa. They never flew in or flew out," Mr Moran said.

"Let's hope that there's never another one.

"As I've said for a long, long time, those 151 workers deserve to be remembered, but more importantly they deserve to be memorialised."

Mount Isa Mines underground copper mine closed in July of last year. (Supplied: Mount Isa Mines Photographic Collection/ABC News: Sharon Gordon)

Long time coming

Mount Isa Mayor Peta MacRae said she was proud the long called-for memorial was finally becoming a reality.

"We are hoping to get the sod turned and get underway as soon as we possibly can," Mayor MacRae said.

Peta MacRae says the memorial plans will go to tender as soon as possible. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

She said $700,000 of the funding would be provided by council for the construction of the memorial.

Despite plans and costings being drawn up in 2023, support for the project ultimately stalled without the backing of the previous state government.

Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie said the Crisafulli government would be injecting $2 million into the memorial through repurposed funds from the Mount Isa Transition Fund.

Jarrod Bleijie and mines minister Dale Last say the Queensland government is injecting $2 million into building the miners memorial. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

Mr Bleijie said re-allocating the funds for a memorial site still honoured its original plan of supporting the region's economy after the closure of the Mount Isa underground copper mine in 2025.

"When people are coming to towns like Mount Isa, that's heart and soul is the mining community, they can reflect and be educated on how important the mining industry is in the great state of Queensland," he said.

While there had been no deaths at Mount Isa Mines since Glencore took ownership in 2013, the mining giant is also putting $2 million into the site.

Glencore's Troy WIlson and Maryann Wipaki say bringing the memorial into existence is important for Mount Isa. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

Glencore Metals Chief Operating Officer Troy Wilson began his career at the famed mine in the 1990s and said the mine and local community had been connected for over a century.

"But that history has suffered some profound loss and we must remember every day that there's people that went to work here and didn't get to come home," Mr Wilson said.

"This memorial will create a permanent place where we can honour all those that have gone before.

"It also will stand as an opportunity for us to remember what our responsibility is and that's to learn from the past, to continuously improve, and to ensure we do everything we can every day to make sure all of our workers go home safe at the end of the day."

title: Tex Walker announces retirement from AFL
text:
Adelaide Crows great Taylor "Tex" Walker says he will retire at the end of the AFL season.

A veteran of 316 AFL matches, Walker has kicked a Crows club record of 706 goals.

Walker, 36, has played 19 seasons in the AFL for the Crows, captaining the club from 2015-2019, including to the 2017 grand final.

"As a young kid from Broken Hill, I dreamed about one day playing for the Crows and I'm so grateful to have been able to live that life," Walker said.

"I've shared the journey with so many great teammates, coaches and staff, as well as my family and friends, and I'm incredibly thankful for the role they've played in my career.

"To our members and supporters, thank you for riding every high and low with me, and your unwavering support is one of the reasons this club is such a special place.

"I'm going to leave the game with a great deal of pride, gratitude and a lifetime of memories, not to mention an ongoing sense of belonging to the Crows community."

Walker was drafted by the Crows in 2007, making his debut during the 2009 season.

He earned an all-Australian selection in 2023, and was also named the AFL Players' Association Best Captain in 2016 and 2017.

"Everyone sees the goals and big moments, but those who have worked closely with Tex know the care he has for his teammates, our coaches and staff, and the club," Crows coach Matthew Nicks said.

"He's someone who led through actions as much as words. He was prepared to stand up when things were going well and, importantly, he stood tall when they weren't."

title: Aussie high jumper wins gold at under-20 world titles
text:
Australian high jumper Izobelle Louison-Roe has won gold at the World Athletics U20 Championships.

The 19-year-old came into the championships in Eugene, Oregon as the leading under-20 jumper this year, twice hitting a personal best of 1.95 metres.

She would not need a personal best to win gold on Sunday (local time), with a jump of 1.92m enough to be crowned champion, adding to the silver she won at Lima during the 2024 championships.

Hungary's Lilianna Bátori claimed silver and Spaniard Aitana Alonso won bronze, both jumping 1.90 metres.

"It was such an exciting competition, one of the moments of my life," Louison-Roe said.

"It was an incredible feeling when I won.

"I was crying so much I couldn't keep it together, it was amazing."

Louison-Roe was not the only Australian to medal on Sunday, with the 4x400m relay team securing a silver.

The Aussie quartet of Shari Hurdman, Xanthee Watts, Charlotte McAuliffe and Alice Hill ran a 3:31.39 to finish second behind the United States.

"Honestly, it's surreal to just go out there and get the job done," McAuliffe said post-race.

"I think we knew coming into this what we were all capable of, and we knew a medal was definitely possible.

" To go out and do the job is just amazing. "

Australia's men's 4x400m relay team — Seth Kennedy, Fred Hamblin, Dylan Hall and Chase Grant — came agonisingly close to also winning a medal, missing out on the podium by four-hundredths of a second.

Grant produced a brilliant final leg of 44.85 seconds, but was just pipped at the line by the French runner.

The women's 4x100m team — Thewbelle Philp, Zara Hagan, Grace Crowe and Emilia Reed — were also pipped at the line and placed fourth.

Kieran Shepherd ran a personal best of 3:42.25 to place eighth in the men's 1,500m, while Milla Roberts overcame a mid-race fall to be 14th in the women's 1,500m.

Elijah Wilson placed 13th in the men's discus final with a best throw of 56.47m.

title: AFLW double-header season opener left fans with 'lots of mixed feelings'
text:
As young Carlton star Poppy Scholz launched the ball into the stands at Docklands Stadium to kick the first goal of the 2026 AFLW season, fans were asking each other: "What do you think this crowd is?'"

The Blues were playing against St Kilda in the season opener in one of five double-headers between the men's and women's competitions this season.

Players, clubs and fans have been calling for regular double-headers to be introduced by the AFL to help grow the women's game.

This was in a bid to increase exposure of the women's game, try to adopt more fans across, give a unified club identity (one club, two teams approach) and allow the women to play on better conditions to allow for a better product.

St Kilda puts up a late challenge against Carlton but the Blues never give up their lead. (Getty: Morgan Hancock)

By half-time on Sunday evening there were 11,000 people in the crowd, 2,000 more than the sold-out Australia vs Ireland game at North Sydney Oval a week earlier.

Halfway through the final quarter, that number had ballooned to 20,455.

For St Kilda veteran and former captain Hannah Priest, they gave "a nice unity for an all-club approach".

"I look at the idea of all of your teams playing on the same day and celebrating each other," she told ABC Sport, acknowledging that a lot of club staff worked across both the men's and women's programs.

"To open the season at [Docklands] is a testament to every single AFLW supporter who has advocated for this sort of growth, and everyone who's been on board since the start. It's a celebration for all of us."

Blues' 26-point win over Saints Carlton has held off a St Kilda fightback to claim the opening win of the new AFLW season by 26 points in an entertaining game that made a case for more double header fixtures.

Across the stadium and fan sections, fans enjoyed the pizzazz of the bigger stadium, crowd noise and being sheltered from the rain.

However, there were also some who missed the community element of the suburban grounds and felt like AFLW was the main event.

Carlton AFLW fan Asha Ziffer, who has a membership for the women's team but not the men's, said she probably wouldn't have gone to the double-header had it not been the opener.

"I've got a lot of mixed feelings about it, but I don't think that this showcases it as it should be," Ziffer told ABC Sport.

"I think that it is presenting it as second to the men's game, and certainly for a season opener, W should be the focus."

There were 20,455 in the last quarter of the AFLW opener between St Kilda and Carlton. (Getty: Michael Willson/AFL Photos)

Ziffer said her 14-year-old daughter, Lily, said "it's like when you go to a concert and there's a support act that only half the people come to and then there's the main event".

"I think even if a 14-year-old can identify that, then it does say something more broadly to the community about where the women's game sits," Ziffer said, during the third quarter.

"Look, it's great and the game is going our way, which is great, even better. But it does feel, because it's such a big venue, I think 11,000 turnout is great but it just doesn't feel like a big crowd because the venue is so big. And you know, I'm sure it's a great ground for them to play on. And you know, it's nice to have a roof over our heads, given the weather's average."

Long time AFLW St Kilda fan Shae Williams said although her side didn't come away with the win, she hoped the team left the evening with a few more fans.

"It was exciting walking in and the thought of W starting … [although it] felt weird not being in a more intimate setting like Moorabbin.

"Twenty thousand attendance was a great result [and a] good experience for the players to play on a bigger stage," Williams told ABC Sport.

"The idea of double-headers are great, [although] I understand the need for W to have its own space as well."

Carlton won its opening match against St Kilda at Docklands. (Getty: Morgan Hancock)

Another Saints supporter, Dylan Cross, who got into both the games with his men's and women's membership, was pleased with the early turnout for the women's game.

"I heard a few people comment around me that haven't watched much women's footy that it was better than they expected," Cross told ABC Sport.

"So, hopefully it [double-headers] grow the game.

"I will say personally I still prefer the AFLW games at smaller grounds like Ikon or Moorabbin due to the more local footy vibes and that it's so family friendly. The crowd felt a bit reserved tonight.

"But all in all, I think it was a success and hopefully we see more double-headers in the future."

title: Australia's 'FIFO ghosts' a growing problem on census night
text:
As households across Australia begin filling out their forms for the 2026 Census, mining communities fear the count will fail to capture the nation's growing fly-in fly-out (FIFO) workforce.

The historic mining city of Kalgoorlie-Boulder, about 600 kilometres east of Perth, is experiencing one of the biggest booms in its history.

An aerial view of Kalgoorlie's Super Pit gold mine. (ABC Goldfields: Ivo Da Silva)

The rise in FIFO work practices has been so dramatic that Kalgoorlie-Boulder Airport is now among the busiest in regional WA, with more than half a million passenger movements.

Mayor Glenn Wilson has made regular use of the airport travelling to Canberra to lobby for changes to the census while casting doubt on the accuracy of previous data.

"What we've continually done through lobbying of the ABS [Australian Bureau of Statistics] is to make sure our ghost populations are included," he said.

"We have got a baseline population, and then with the mining activities, those populations increase and put added strain on our infrastructure and our services."

He chairs the Australian Mining Cities Alliance, which counts the City of Broken Hill, City of Karratha, Mount Isa City Council, Isaac Regional Council and the Shire of East Pilbara among its members.

Glenn Wilson is concerned "ghost populations" are not being included in the data. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

FIFO boom at airport

When the first national census was held in 1911, the population of Kalgoorlie and Boulder, then separate towns, was estimated at a combined 19,605.

That grew to 29,306 as of the 2021 Census, with 20 per cent of the population employed in gold mining.

According to the latest ABS data, Kalgoorlie-Boulder's population was 31,268 at June 30 last year.

An aerial view of the Kalgoorlie CBD. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Mr Wilson estimates there could be as many as 10,000 FIFO workers in Kalgoorlie-Boulder due to the current boom.

"We know since the last census there's been more dwellings built in Kalgoorlie-Boulder, there are less rentals available, less houses for sale, so if this data comes back and tells us our population is going south, there is an issue with how the census is done," he said.

"Why is it important? Because funding opportunities at a state and federal level rely on up-to-date population figures.

"An increase in population gives us more opportunity to get more funding. It's as simple as that, because many of the grant mechanisms take your population into account."

Passengers line up for security screening at Kalgoorlie-Boulder Airport. (Supplied: Cass Be)

Kalgoorlie-Boulder Airport was built for 100,000 passenger movements a year back in the early 1990s.

City of Kalgoorlie-Boulder figures show there were 562,710 passenger movements in the 12 months to June 30, eclipsing the previous year's record of 458,876 passengers.

"Based on the airport figures, I am very optimistic we're going to see a population increase," Mr Wilson said.

FIFO workers on the tarmac at Karratha Airport. (ABC News: Cody Fenner)

Similar concerns in Pilbara

The FIFO workforce has been a long-term feature of the iron ore heartland of WA's Pilbara, where the 2021 Census put the population at 82,000.

But Regional Development Australia's Pilbara chief executive Daiva Gillam said infrastructure was struggling to meet the needs of the local and FIFO population.

"I'm going to give you a real-world example," she said.

"The Shire of East Pilbara in Newman are spending over $50 million of their own money to upgrade the wastewater treatment plant because it can't cope.

"For every person in Newman that lives there, there are up to three FIFOs all flushing the toilet in the East Pilbara.

"The infrastructure is not built to cope, but those workers aren't usually counted in the Pilbara as being residents."

Newman sits in WA's east Pilbara region. (ABC Pilbara: Charlie McLean)

Robert Powell is on a two and one roster, working two weeks in Port Hedland as a groundsperson at a camp and spending the week off in Perth.

Despite spending more time up north, he will list his Perth home as his primary residence.

"Home is home, work is work, and it needs to be reflected that way in the census," he said.

"It's, to me, no different to saying I live in Armadale and work in Welshpool. It's where I live, it's where I want the services provided."

He suggested adding more questions to the census would help properly account for the FIFO workforce.

Workers leave a FIFO flight at Karratha Airport. (ABC News: Cody Fenner)

How are FIFO workers counted?

Census spokesperson Emily Walter said FIFO workers were similar to seasonal farm workers, who can be a challenging demographic to collect data on.

She said the ABS had employed a dedicated team to coordinate with mine sites to enable workers to complete the census in the most accurate way.

"The census creates a snapshot at a point in time, like taking a photograph," she said.

"FIFO workers are often in a location for several days or weeks at a time, and the concept of a usual residence is one that we use to capture where someone is for more than six months of the year.

"If they are spending more than six months of the year at the location where they work, then they need to use that as their usual residence.

"That 'usual residence' concept is something that is really important for how we understand the data, and an internationally comparable definition."

A matter of 'belonging'

Organisational psychiatrist Cheryl Yam said the question ran deeper than data for affected FIFO workers.

"The question isn't simply 'where do I sleep most nights?' It's more where do I belong?" she said.

Cities like Kalgoorlie previously relied on a chiefly residential workforce, but the FIFO population is growing. (ABC News: Erin Parke)

"The camp really isn't necessarily home, but it's also more than just a workplace; because it's where they spend much of their day-to-day life."

Dr Yam said workers often felt the remote camp was where they stayed and home being where they lived.

Officials understand the sentiment, but say the workforce and infrastructure pressures across regional Australia meant every worker needed to be accurately counted.

In keeping with that growth theme, Ms Gillam said it was vital for regional areas that every worker was counted.

"Nobody wants to say that they live where they work," she said.

"But for the purpose of the census only, if you're here for six months, yeah, this is where you live."

The census data is scheduled to be released in June 2027.

title: Carlton fans chant 'we want Fraser', talks on coaching future imminent
text:
Carlton fans are chanting Josh Fraser's name and a similar endorsement from the club's hierarchy for the Blues' interim coach to take the reins full time could follow as soon as this week.

Fraser has mounted an irrepressible case to take on the vacant head coach role, having delivered 10 wins and just two losses since stepping up when Michael Voss was sacked in mid-May, with the Blues at 1-8.

The interim coach, who earned "we want Fraser" chants from Carlton fans after last night's 44-point win, is yet to officially throw his hat in the ring — but that conversation is imminent.

Loading...

"At some stage this week there'll be an opportunity to have some conversations with the club," Fraser said.

"It'll be sometime this week."

Half-back Adam Cerra joked whether the interim boss taking the reins was the hardest question at the club at the moment.

"Obviously the club's got their processes. We've got full faith in that process and their decision and we'll support whatever they pick. 'Frase' has been great," he said.

"The boys obviously love playing with him. We'll leave that to the club."

Cerra put Carlton's turnaround down to a combination of Fraser's influence and how the playing group lifted him — with experienced players leading from the front and young players expressing themselves.

"Frase has probably allowed a bit of freedom for us to do that, a bit of simplicity in the way we're trying to play," Cerra said.

"It hasn't set too many boundaries on us. It's more trying to explore what our best football looks like and building that week to week.

"These last couple of weeks we've been getting more confidence in our process and our trust and executing."

Fraser was asked whether part of his thinking in holding off on nominating was around managing if he missed out on the job while preparing the team for a potential wildcard match.

Blues plant one foot in the AFL finals as Saints lose star to hamstring Carlton plants one foot in the AFL finals series with a statement victory over the Saints at Docklands.

"It's a fair question, but no, I haven't thought too deeply about that," the 43-year-old said.

"I've just tried to stay as narrow as I can and it's been challenging with a lot of the questioning and different things, but I still feel such a responsibility to this role as interim coach.

"That's what I needed to, and have, focused all of my energy on — because I would be doing a disservice, not only to our players, but our staff and everyone, if I started to stray away from that.

"Clearly I've had to think through some things, but that hasn't occupied a lot of my thinking and all the hypotheticals haven't either. Most of my energy has been focused on this playing group and footy club."

The Blues sit eight points clear in 10th with games against the Western Bulldogs and Fremantle to come.

"[It's] not about daring to dream, I think the thing that's taking us forward is we are just attaching ourselves to the work that we need to do," Fraser said.

AAP

title: Sydney Airport near miss 'could have been far more serious', ATSB boss says
text:
Pilots who avoided a second near miss at Sydney Airport in a fortnight "prevented what could have been far more serious", the head of the nation's air safety bureau says.

The comments from Australian Transport Safety Bureau's Chief Commissioner Angus Mitchell come just a day after a Jetstar flight almost collided with a Qatar Airways flight.

"We do know that in both the incidents, two weeks ago and again yesterday, it was the actions of the pilots on board that prevented what could have been far more serious," Mr Mitchell told the ABC on Monday.

Commissioner Mitchell says the investigation will look into whether any individual errors were made. (Supplied: ATSB)

Commissioner Mitchell said an incident like last weekend's "shouldn't happen".

"We do have an aviation sector that is the envy of the world. That's not to say that with incidents like this, we don't take them seriously to improve," he said.

"But aircraft movements, whether it be in a busy airport or in the skies, are incredibly well coordinated here in Australia."

Emergency meetings will be held in Canberra on Monday as an investigation gets underway into Sunday's near-miss, which followed days of flight disruptions and delays.

Two airport workers were stood down pending the outcome of an official investigation into the near collision, which left a Jetstar crew member injured yesterday.

Two airport workers involved in Sunday's near miss have since been stood down. (Supplied)

Jetstar flight JQ402 was preparing to take off for the Gold Coast and was taxiing to the runway when it was forced to slam on the brakes.

Its flight crew noticed a Qatar Airways plane that was being towed along the tarmac by an aircraft tug and in close proximity.

Both aircraft stopped abruptly, avoiding crashing by mere metres.

Describing it as "extremely concerning", federal Transport Minister Catherine King vowed any "systemic issues" to come out of the investigation by the aviation safety watchdog would be addressed.

She also said Airservices Australia "needs to do better" to manage disruptions at the airport, which has grappled with a shortage of air traffic controllers.

Thousands of passengers were affected by lengthy delays over recent days, with some missing flight connections as a result.

"They caused significant challenges to passengers, staff and airlines," Ms King said.

" My office has asked for an explanation, and for Airservices to outline a pathway to improve the delivery of its services. "

It was understood the organisation's CEO Rob Sharp will meet with her this morning in Canberra.

Airservices Australia, the government-owned body responsible for safely and efficiently managing air traffic, said yesterday in a statement that Air Traffic Flow Management measures had been put in place following the incident, including departure spacing "to safely manage projected airborne and departure demands".

"Airservices is reviewing the incident and will assist with any safety investigation," it said

Investigation underway

A Jetstar spokesperson said the aircraft had been following air traffic control instructions before its pilots brought the plane to a sudden stop. (ABC News: Peter Garnish)

Chief Commissioner Mitchell on Sunday said it was too early to know the cause of the near miss with investigators examining all possibilities, including one line of inquiry that the tug pulling the aircraft did not follow Air Traffic Control instructions.

"Now exactly why they came so close is I guess really what we're trying to understand at the moment so we're gathering the evidence we need to make that determination," he said.

"So that will be from both the pilots on board the Jetstar aircraft, those that were controlling the Qatar plane, as well as those in the coordination of air traffic control, to understand what potentially broke down in the coordination or communication.

A shortage of air traffic controllers at Sydney Airport is affecting services, the Civil Air boss says. (ABC News)

It was the second near miss at the airport in recent weeks, with two Qantas planes narrowly avoiding crashing late last month.

Commissioner Mitchell said in both instances the pilots were able to act quickly to avoid a collision.

He said the probe would be wide-ranging and also scrutinise whether the understaffing issues within the airport's air traffic control fleet had any role to play.

Commissioner Mitchell said the investigation needed to uncover whether systemic changes were needed to ensure that if individual errors are made, that there are other mechanisms in place to avoid serious problems.

'There aren't enough controllers'

The government confirmed the air traffic control ground worker and the tug operator involved in yesterday's near collision have both been stood down, pending the outcome of the investigation.

A Jetstar spokesperson said the aircraft had been following air traffic control instructions during the incident and its captain acted "quickly and decisively".

The crew member sustained a minor injury after falling when the pilot hit the brakes.

The boss of the union representing air traffic controllers declined to publicly comment what he believed was the cause of the two near collisions, saying it was "premature" while investigations were underway.

Mr Nugent said resourcing for air traffic controllers has been a long-running issue. (Supplied)

But Civil Air president Scott Nugent, who is a trained air traffic controller, said staffing shortages took a heavy toll on those working on the frontline.

"What I can say is that air traffic controllers in Australia are working very hard, and for a long time they have not necessarily had the resources they need to do their jobs properly," he told the ABC.

"There aren't enough controllers in Australia."

He said the air traffic control system at Sydney Airport relied on workers doing excessive overtime, with some potentially doing more than 20 extra hours a week.

"We've seen in the past few days what happened when you don't have enough air traffic controllers, the impact on industry," he said.

"Civil Air has been saying to Airservices over the past four or five years you don't have enough air traffic controllers in Sydney airport tower.

"No matter why they occurred, people no longer want to work the overtime because they're very stressed and upset, and the whole system is propped up on overtime."

Mr Nugent said he would also be meeting with Mr Sharp later today to discuss his concerns in the wake of the weekend disruption.

title: Live: Former Japanese ambassador warns PM over 'insulting' melon gesture
text:
People might well be asking why there's a bit of a flurry over the prime minister's "melons" gaffe right now, given the podcast happened weeks ago.

It's worth noting that nobody in the Japanese government has said a word publicly about Anthony Albanese's remark since he made it.

Some officials may well have winced in private, but Australia is a critical energy partner for Japan, and an increasingly important security partner as well.

At a time when Japan is deeply worried about global energy disruptions, and the long-term security threat presented by China (as well as North Korea and Russia) it is unlikely to spend too much time dwelling on a tacky comment on a podcast.

As one Japanese official put it to the ABC a little while back, loosely paraphrased: yes it was unfortunate, but we have real problems to worry about right now.

The episode has also barely caused a ripple in the Japanese press, aside from one scathing opinion piece in the English language Japan Times which lambasted Albanese and accused him of rank sexism.

Shingo Yamagami's intervention could shift the equation here — particularly because (as the former ambassador points out) Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has already copped sexist attacks from Chinese state media.

Will his op-ed kick off a round of media reaction in Australia which then sparks a corresponding media flurry in Japan, forcing a political response in Canberra and Tokyo?

We'll have to wait and see.

But it's also worth noting Yamagami has some history with the ALP, and didn't exactly enjoy a close relationship with Albanese or Penny Wong after Labor claimed power in 2022.

He was particularly angry when Wong urged him (while still in opposition) to pull back his public criticisms of China while he was Japan's ambassador in Canberra — an intervention he clearly saw as unacceptable.

title: Big changes for NSW renters as portable bond scheme begins
text:
From today, renters moving into selected New South Wales suburbs can transfer their existing bonds to their new rental properties, potentially saving thousands of dollars.

The government's Smart Rental Bonds scheme is now live, but currently it is only available in the Parramatta, Penrith and Central Coast local government areas.

The system is being introduced a year later than expected and it won't be free to use, but the government thinks it will be popular with renters.

What is the scheme?

Smart Rental Bonds is designed to remove one of the financial headaches many renters experience when they are moving from one property to another.

Having been accepted for a rental, they may be required to find thousands of dollars to pay a bond for the new property before their old bond is returned to them.

Shelter NSW CEO John Engeler said the stress of finding cash to cover another bond can be a major barrier to moving.

"It might seem like it's not a big deal, but for people on low and very low incomes, this is a game changer," he said.

John Engeler calls the scheme a "game changer". (Supplied: Homes NSW)

Some tenants have to borrow money, he added, or go without food in order to scrape together another deposit.

To overcome this, Smart Rental Bonds allows renters to transfer their existing bond to their new property via an online portal.

How does it work？

Renters will have to pay a $25 application fee to use the online service, overseen by NSW Fair Trading.

They will have to nominate which bond they would like to transfer, choose where they want it sent, then pay the difference if the new bond is higher.

For example, if the existing bond is $2,400 but the new bond is $2,700, the tenant will need to make a $300 top-up payment in order to transfer it.

If the new bond is cheaper than the existing one, the tenant will be refunded as long as no claim is made against the existing bond.

How do landlords make claims against the bond？

The process of deducting money from a bond will not fundamentally change for the landlord.

If a landlord believes they are owed money due to unpaid rent or damage, they can make a claim against the bond.

If the tenant agrees to the claim, the government will pay the landlord directly and the renter will have to pay the government back within 28 days.

The process for landlords for deducting money from a bond will not change. (ABC News: Jack Ailwood)

If the tenant disputes the claim, the matter can be determined by the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (NCAT).

The government will only pay a landlord's claim once there is an agreement with the tenant or an order from NCAT.

Who can use it？

For now, only renters moving into properties in the Parramatta, Penrith and Central Coast local government areas can use Smart Rental Bonds.

Fair Trading Minister Anoulack Chanthivong said the scheme needed to be scaled up gradually.

"You're talking close to a million bonds and $2.3 billion worth of renters' money," he said.

" Having a planned, phased process ensures that the system works smoothly and actually instils trust and confidence. "

Anoulack Chanthivong says there are about a million bonds in NSW worth $2.3 billion. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

The government had hoped to deliver the scheme by late 2025, but delayed its launch until mid-2026 to ensure it could roll out smoothly.

Mr Chanthivong said more locations would be added in the coming months.

"If things go well, every renter across New South Wales will have access to Smart Rental Bonds by the end of the year."

Why the fee？

The $25 fee is payable every time a renter wants to transfer their bond.

While the scheme has been welcomed by the Tenants' Union of NSW, the fee has not.

When the government announced the details earlier this year, the Tenants' Union said the $25 charge would disproportionately affect renters on low incomes.

The online rental bond service will cost renters $25. (ABC News)

Mr Chanthivong said the fee would help cover the scheme's administration costs and insisted the government wasn't trying to profit.

"It's a very small investment from renters of $25, which potentially saves them up to $4,000," he said.

Mr Engeler said while he would prefer the scheme to be free, he believed the application fee would be worth it.

"At $25, I think most reasonable people would say that's a lot less of an impediment than $2,500 or what an average four-week bond would be," he said.

"Let's not worry about the cents. We're talking about big dollars."

Brian To’o and Jarome Luai are set to reunite in PNG. title: A ticket to the Neil Diamond musical might as well be a ticket for a time machine
text:
Advertisement

Key points MUSICALS: A Beautiful Noise: The Neil Diamond Musical arrives in Melbourne

THEATRE: Pummel Squad’s Marginalia at fortyfivedownstairs is outlandish and camp

MUSIC: Sheku Kanneh-Mason performs with the MSO in a tranformative show

MUSIC: Laufey puts on a five-star show at Rod Laver Arena

DANCE: The internet meets live performance in CreepyPasta at Dancehouse

MUSICALS

A Beautiful Noise: The Neil Diamond Musical ★★★★

Princess Theatre, until October 25 I was still in the womb in February 1976, when Neil Diamond – at the height of his powers – enthralled a 14,000-strong crowd at Melbourne’s Sidney Myer Music Bowl. Another 5000 were crammed against the fence outside the venue, peeking through gaps in the hessian, and one excited reviewer described the concert as “D-Day”, noting that Diamond, “dressed in brown leather trousers … and a pink shirt, won [fans over] even before he reached centre stage”. Will Swenson as a young Neil Diamond Ruby Alexander Fifty years on, the Australian premiere of A Beautiful Noise has opened at the Princess Theatre, and it will most definitely appeal to veterans of “D-Day”, or anyone who saw the music legend perform live. Sure, it mightn’t fuse rock biography and music catalogue with the same theatrical completeness as the highest level of jukebox musical – as in Jersey Boys, or more recently Tina – but the show delivers the goods as an act of charismatic resurrection.

Advertisement

Will Swenson, who originated the role on Broadway, gives a pitch-perfect vocal and histrionic impersonation – one that channels the genius, personality, and emotional range of this singular artist with such “gravel wrapped in velvet” accuracy that a ticket to the show might as well be a ticket for a time machine. That idea synchs with the awkward, if beautifully acted, framing device, in which a much older and more troubled Diamond (Terence Crawford) works through his issues with a psychiatrist (Monica Sayers), and revisits significant events in his career and personal life. Ashleigh Rubenach as Marcia Murphey and Will Swenson as Neil Diamond in A Beautiful Noise: The Neil Diamond Musical. Ruby Alexander The past emerges with surreal razzle-dazzle. Choruses dressed in a motley collection of ’60s countercultural fashions, or silver lamé and sequins from the ’70s, leap out from behind the psychiatrist’s couch and burst into song, with a younger Diamond in tow. Moments of heartbreak during his first two marriages – to Jaye Posner (Alana Tranter) and Marcia Murphey (Ashleigh Rubenach) – are well-served by the melancholy side of the playlist, with break-up ballads such as Love on the Rocks and You Don’t Bring Me Flowers.

Advertisement

They’re balanced by more upbeat numbers that chart Diamond’s rise to superstardom: Diamond’s discovery by producer Ellie Greenwich (Hannah Fredericksen); the years spent writing hits made famous by other artists (I’m A Believer and Red Red Wine, for starters); and his breakout as a solo artist, via an ill-considered encounter with a mobster-owned record label, and an intimate live music venue named The Bitter End. Related Article Stage shows ‘Good times never felt so good’: A peek behind the curtain of the new Neil Diamond musical Once the music icon reaches a stratospheric level of wealth and fame, the narrative recedes and a live concert vibe overtakes it, with the odd flashback to his origin story (Diamond is the son of Jewish immigrant parents), the toll that her husband’s constant touring takes on his second wife, and predictable progress towards self-awareness with his psych, made less annoying by Crawford’s terrifically growly baritone rendition of I Am … I Said. As a tribute to Neil Diamond, A Beautiful Noise does exactly what it says on the jukebox. It’s full of spectacle and humour, emotion and nostalgia, and of course, the music. I suspect most Boomers will love it as much as my mum did, but subsequent generations (especially those of us for whom bawling the chorus to Sweet Caroline at suburban parties was a rite of passage) should get a kick out of it, too.

Reviewed by Cameron Woodhead

Advertisement

THEATRE

Marginalia ★★★

Pummel Squad, fortyfivedownstairs, until August 16 Ukrainian writer Nikolai Gogol is best known in the theatre world for his satire of corruption and cronyism, The Government Inspector. But his short story The Nose has powdered itself for the limelight in recent years – most memorably in Barrie Kosky’s vaudevillian production of the Shostakovich opera based on the tale, which featured a chorus of giant noses tap-dancing between acts. Marginalia is as rich in grotesque spectacle as poor theatre could be Nick Robertson Indie theatre collective Pummel Squad doesn’t have the budget for that, of course, but its outlandish camp adaptation, Marginalia, is as rich in grotesque spectacle as poor theatre could be. This version begins with an artist who moonlights as a barber (Ludomyr Kemp-Mykyta) running in circles to Fatboy Slim’s ’90s rave anthem Right Here, Right Now.

Advertisement

It’s comically pointless performance art, interrupted by gun-toting guerrillas and the accidental shooting of a passing clown (Molly Holohan), who gives a hilariously extended dying monologue before giving up the ghost. Then, the artist finds a dismembered nose in his sandwich, just as an army officer arrives… There is a fearless commitment to caricature and slapstick and inane farce Nick Robertson Elsewhere, a vain bureaucrat known as Major Pepsi (Cooper Donald McDonald) awakens without a nose. He can’t hide such a thing from his loyal manservant (AYA) or his monstrous mother (Alexandra Aldrich) and embarks on a frenetic quest to get his nose back. Satirical episodes from the original are revamped into a mix of camp contemporary Australian and Imperial Russian satire. Pepsi tries to get a wanted poster for his nose printed, but the clerk (Harry McGee) won’t help, so he foments revolution in the queue (assisted by an ancient Russian babushka) with lewd results.

Advertisement

A church service transmutes into a queer orgy. Torture scenes play out in some basement of the Lubyanka. And the nose grows to human size, attains a higher rank than Pepsi and gallivants away, leading to a face-off at the governor-general’s ball. The final line of Gogol’s story asserts the reality of the tall tale he has created. Here, we get the clash of naked self-interest between bureaucrat and artist – a conflict that artists are almost always bound to lose. Editor's pick Visual art A painting in which a man sleeps while the world burns has won a $100,000 art prize I didn’t love every change and some modern themes lurking in the original – food inflation, fake news – don’t get picked up. Still, most revisions are wildly or grimly inspired, and director Katy Maudlin directs a cast with a fearless commitment to caricature and slapstick and inane farce. Alongside marvellously silly costumes, it makes for an entertaining ride through a world that’s stopped making sense.

Advertisement

With six full-length shows (plus an annual Christmas pantomime) since it was founded in 2023, Pummel Squad is a significant company. I’ll be sure to sniff out future work.

Reviewed by Cameron Woodhead MUSIC

Sheku Kanneh-Mason x MSO ★★★★

Hamer Hall, August 6 When Sheku Kanneh-Mason touches his bow to the cello strings, something transformative happens. There is no separation between the British musician and his instrument; they melt into a singularity. His face transforms while playing, vibrating with the feeling of it all. Sheku Kanneh-Mason’s face transforms while he plays the cello, as the MSO swells and sighs behind him. Laura Manariti The 27-year-old is one of classical music’s bright young stars, with an impressive CV including a solo performance at the 2018 wedding of Prince Harry and Meghan Markle. He is in Melbourne performing the Australian premiere of British composer Edmund Finnis’ cello concerto, written especially for him and co-commissioned by international orchestras including the Melbourne Symphony Orchestra.

Advertisement

The cello is, of course, the central feature of the work – Finnis played the instrument himself in his youth, and has tapped into its many possibilities in his composition. There are nods to the past – the first movement is built around arpeggiated motifs that feel like a contemporary version of Bach’s famous cello prelude – alongside more distinctly modern elements. Kanneh-Mason proves the diversity of the instrument’s sound, from soulful singing to almost violent double-stops; he hits a few dud notes in the higher register but seamlessly recovers, and when the cello soars alone, it’s transcendent. Elsewhere, the MSO swells and sighs behind him, picking up the pace in the busy third movement to build to a rapturous finale. Conductor Jaime Martín leads the orchestra through a dynamic and exciting program that includes Tchaikovsky’s Symphony No. 5. Laura Manariti He is all smiles when it ends, encoring with a short solo that again showcases his winning combination of control and emotion. You can sense the audience craves more. But that’s all from him. Sheku-Mason’s performance is bookended by the orchestra playing Debussy’s Prélude à l’après-midi d’un faune and Tchaikovsky’s Symphony No. 5.

Advertisement

Under conductor Jaime Martín, the Tchaikovsky in particular is dynamic and exciting, with muscular brass adding dramatic texture. The cello’s range is again on display through the symphony – a walking bass line at one point, sonorous beauty at another. From old to new and back again, this was a special night of music.

Reviewed by Giselle Au-Nhien Nguyen MUSIC

Laufey | A Matter of Time Tour ★★★★★

Rod Laver Arena, until August 1 Ever dated someone and found them so boring, you wondered what you were doing there? That’s what Laufey asked us halfway through her first night back in Melbourne. The Icelandic-Chinese artist sits on the stairs built onto her stage, casually chatting to the crowd before launching into Bored . Laufey performs at Rod Laver Arena, July 30, 2026. Richard Clifford Laufey, 27, has cracked the code for making jazz a staple for her generation. She found fame online – from original work like debut single Street by Street, to jazz standard covers Misty and It’s Been a Long, Long Time. Then came three nights in the Palais Theatre in 2024, before a massive upgrade to Rod Laver Arena in 2026.

Advertisement

The bright, whimsical Lover Girl comes early in Act I (across the show, silent movie-style projections divide the show into acts). Laufey twirls, claps and bounces in a blue dress straight from a fairytale book, and later moves across a castle-like stage structure for Dreamer – half damsel in distress, half determined girl-boss. This act extends beyond the stage. Like any pop fandom, the uniform is clear – here, it’s coquette. Bows, earthy colours or pastels, then flowy skirts, or yellow or blue felt crowns. “I should’ve brought my bunny costume,” says one fan before the show, referring to Mei Mei the Bunny, the main character of the musician’s children’s book. 27-year-old Laufey has cracked the code for making jazz a staple for her generation. Richard Clifford Like any star with an ever-giving pop fandom, Laufey descends to high-five the crowd in Bored, and returns with a fan-made Australian flag with her face on it. “Revolution chic!” she reacts, one of her many witty one-liners of the night. “Hamilton could never.” She crowns a best-dressed fan, and shouts out two fans dressed as coffee and pie, a nod to Let You Break My Heart Again. Seriously, it doesn’t get any more jazz-pop than this.

Advertisement

Act II brings us back to Laufey’s roots. A cover of Old Devil Moon, then jazz remixes of Haunted, Valentine, and Fragile. Her aura shifts from a twirling lover girl to an alluring vocalist as the stage becomes her jazz bar. The circus-like third act brings us Carousel, and the Swan Lake-esque Forget-Me-Not – an ode to her home, Iceland. After an outfit change in Act IV, Laufey emerges in a showman-like set for an abundance of sass in Mr Eclectic, Madwoman and Tough Luck. This one’s a real emotional rollercoaster – she returns to the piano for Promise, the ultimate tear-jerker of the night. Laufey twirls, claps, and bounces in a blue dress straight from a fairytale book. Richard Clifford As always, Laufey continues to flex a widely ranged classical upbringing. She plays a guitar in Falling Behind, a piano in Too Little, Too Late, and plays the cello alongside twin and creative director Junia on the violin for Madwoman. Before closing the act with From the Start, Laufey gets vulnerable about her struggle with beauty standards in Snow White. Perhaps the key to making jazz and bossa nova mainstream among Laufey’s generation, myself included, all boils down to relatability.

Advertisement

A first crush, being “too much”, the most boring or character-altering relationship in your 20s, and struggling with body image – these are some core experiences she sings about. And perhaps we sing along to sing the feelings out. It’s therapeutic, vulnerable and heartfelt, especially in a crowd of thousands. The night ends on a dark, ear-piercing note: Sabotage. The track that jump-scared the internet upon release. Whatever I heard when I flinched on my first listen, it was louder and more intense tonight. Three words sit on my notes app here: “WHAT THE HELL”. Editor's pick Melbourne live reviews The success of a one-woman show lives and dies by its lead. This performer rises to the challenge The encore is surprisingly intimate for a pop show. The stage and orchestra rest for the night, and it’s just Laufey, her guitar, and us. She says bye (for now) with Letter To My 13-Year-Old Self, and fulfils a fan’s request to sing Slow Down. Laufey’s songs are intimate and warm; they feel right for a quiet day at home or a cafe on a rainy day. But her tour shows that her quiet can be loud, that intimacy can be scaled up – and that you sure as hell can belt out bossa nova and jazz – and maybe think about an ex or a crush – for four entire acts.

Reviewed by Gabriela Sumampow

Advertisement

DANCE

CreepyPasta ★★

Dancehouse, until August 8 Creepypastas, for those who don’t know, are short but crude horror stories posted on the internet. And they really are awful. The prose is awkward, the pacing erratic and the content banal. Of course, that’s part of their grubby folkish charm: these are disposable, authorless texts, copied and pasted from forum to forum. Large LED screens loom large in Creepypasta. Darren Gill Can live performance create a creepypasta analogue? Unfortunately, yes. Harrison Hall and his new-media accomplices have pretty much nailed it. Its opening scene is the most effective. Three large LED screens face away from us, their dark backs looming over performer and co-choreographer Nikki Tarling. She, too, faces away, attached by a rope to one screen. Is she umbilically tethered to the machine?

Advertisement

It is a potent image, especially with the red status lights on the backs of the screens staring like little eyes. But once the screens are wheeled around, video content gradually takes over the performance. The live elements – dance and clowning – feel underdeveloped. Some of the material is comic, such as a video using Google Maps to explore the streets around the venue. And some of the material is more challenging, such as the lurid collages of digital detritus, which are accelerated and convulsive, and hard to watch for any length of time. Harrison Hall’s antics resemble creepypasta cosplay more than an embodied critique of technological alienation. Darren Gill Hall, meanwhile, naked except for a long, lank white wig, capers madly about the stage, and into the audience. He has plenty of energy, but there’s not much choreography. His antics resemble creepypasta cosplay more than an embodied critique of technological alienation. Perhaps all this is as it should be: a work modelled on creepypasta should be misshapen, excessive and slightly embarrassing. CreepyPasta captures the internet’s ugliness; as dance theatre, however, it is superfluous because we never see that ugliness landing in the body.

A first home buyer couple paid $850,000 for an Artarmon apartment on Saturday which they had not seen before the day of the auction, picking it up for less than the $925,000 the sellers had paid for the home. The two-bedroom home with cheery feature walls and no parking at 1/36 Hampden Road last traded in 2023 and this time sold for $75,000 less. The property was one of 520 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney last week. By Saturday evening, Domain Group recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 50 per cent from 292 reported results throughout the week, while 94 auctions were withdrawn. A family wanting to be closer to schools paid $1,805,000 for an Essendon family home at auction on Saturday. The renovated four-bedroom house with sleek kitchen and putting green at 186 Napier Street sold above guide of $1.6 million to $1.68 million and the $1.75 million reserve set on auction day. There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide. The property was one of 627 scheduled to go to auction in Melbourne last week. By Saturday evening, Domain Group recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 63 per cent from 465 reported results throughout the week, while 62 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate.

Jellis Craig Essendon’s Christian Lonzi said five bidders registered for the auction and three competed for the keys. The bidding opened at $1.6 million, with the buyers, a family wanting to be closer to the nearby schools, making the opening offer. A salvo of bids followed, some in increments of $20,000 and $10,000 and some as low as $1000.

The final, winning bid was $5000. Lonzi said the vendors, who had owned the property since 2020, had undertaken a renovation on the bathroom and kitchen, which made it attractive to buyers. The clearance rate, which pointed to a more balanced market in Melbourne, was due to a lack of new homes for sale, Lonzi said. “I think what it is, is a lack of a stock at the moment, but that will be a temporary thing,” he said. “I imagine more stock will come onto the market over spring. “The challenge is going to be that spring is before the [state] election. “It has been sluggish in Port Melbourne but over the weekend it seems there was a lot more buyer activity,” he said. “I think people have realised this is the new normal for prices … people still have to buy.” In the popular north-east suburb of Eaglemont, a four-bedroom house at 24 Glenard Drive sold for $1,755,000 after passing in at auction. title: Trump bought Japan some time but the alarm bells are ringing
text:
Advertisement

BusinessMarketsJapan Opinion Trump bought Japan some time but the alarm bells are ringing Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist August 10, 2026 — 11:59am

August 10, 2026 — 11:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The impact of last week’s dramatic interventions in currency markets by the Bank of Japan and the US Treasury to boost Japan’s yen seems to be fading. They might have to intervene again, and again. The US and Japan acted to prop up the yen – for the first time since the 1998 Asian financial crisis – after it crashed through the 162 yen-to-the-dollar level regarded as the BoJ’s “line in the sand” last month, and kept heading northward. Before the intervention, the yen/dollar cross-rate was almost 164 yen to the dollar. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and US President Donald Trump in the White House in March. Bloomberg Over two days last week, the BoJ spent an estimated $US87 billion ($123.2 billion) and the US Treasury up to $US10 billion to buy yen, which drove the exchange rate up to a peak of 155.21 yen to the dollar. The exchange rate has since slipped back to just over 157.7, after hitting 158.40 on Friday. In the absence of further interventions, Japan’s economic fundamentals – the influences which had driven its currency down – could be expected to reassert themselves.

Advertisement

Those are its extreme levels of government debt (more than 200 per cent of GDP, albeit that about half that is owned by the government itself after decades of bond buying), rising inflation and, despite being on track to post a budget surplus, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s plan to cut consumption taxes and significantly boost spending on defence and technology. Related Article Opinion

Trump's America Fool’s gold: Trump is set to break his promise to America Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Most significant are Japan’s suppressed bond yields, with the BoJ having orchestrated a negative real interest rate regime for much of the past three decades, during an economic winter from which Japan is only just emerging. The BoJ’s policy rate, at 1 per cent, compares with the US Federal Reserve Board’s target for the federal funds rate of between 3.5 per cent and 3.75 per cent and the Reserve Bank’s cash rate of 4.35 per cent. Two-year Japanese government bonds yield 1.6 per cent, 10-year bonds 2.79 per cent and 30-year bonds 3.91 per cent. Their US counterparts yield 4.2 per cent, 4.65 per cent and 5.2 per cent, respectively.

Advertisement

Those large differentials have encouraged Japanese investors to export their savings in pursuit of higher returns and created the multi-trillion dollar “carry trade,” where hedge funds and others have borrowed at negligible cost in Japan to invest in higher-yielding assets offshore. As long as the yield differentials remain as large as they are now, the yen is destined to remain weak against the dollar, aiding Japan’s exports but importing inflation. A rise in US yields, a function of the continuing increase in US government debt levels, which has accelerated under the second Trump administration, as well as US inflation levels that have been pushed higher by Trump’s tariffs and his war in the Middle East, has intensified the pressure on the exchange rate. The most obvious reason for the US decision to intervene is that, if the BoJ were forced to raise Japan’s interest rates to support the yen – and bond yields have been edging up in the market already – the vast hoard of Japanese capital now invested in the US, more than $US1.1 trillion of it in US Treasury bonds, might start flowing back to Japan.

Advertisement

Related Article Retail ‘People want something more than value’: Why we’re so into buying Japanese stuff That would put pressure on the US dollar and, more particularly, upward pressure on US bond yields and administration’s interest costs, which are already above $US1 trillion a year and are the fastest-rising expenditures in the US budget. A weaker yen would also make Japan’s exports to the US more competitive. With the yen also influencing other Asian currencies, that could undermine Trump’s efforts to use tariffs and coerced investment deals to rebuild US manufacturing (not that those efforts have produced anything meaningful yet). While the US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, has pointed to the potential contagion effects of a weak yen and the risk that it could destabilise other currencies in the region, his worst fears would inevitably relate to the implications for the US bond market and the risk that an exodus of capital as investments were repatriated and carry trades unwound might pose a threat to the US economy and US financial stability.

Advertisement

His sensitivity to the US domestic implications of a weakening yen were underscored by the decision to offer the BoJ a Federal Reserve “repo” facility – it has borrowed Fed-printed dollars, using the US treasuries it owns as collateral – rather than risk the Japanese central bank having to dump those holdings to fund its interventions, which would cause US rates to rise further. What the BoJ and US Treasury have done so far is to buy some time. What the US intervention signals is the mutual vulnerabilities of the US and Japan and the reality that reducing them, if they can be reduced, won’t be either straightforward, painless or riskless. Bloomberg By themselves, the interventions might have driven some short sellers from the market and relieved some of the pressure on the currency, but Bessent, who headed the London office of Soros Fund Management when George Soros and Stanley Druckenmiller “broke the pound” and forced in out of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism in 1992, would be very aware that nothing fundamental has changed and the yen remains extremely vulnerable to an assault by traders. The most obvious next step is for the BoJ to raise its policy rate at its September monetary policy meeting, which it might well do despite Sanae Takaichi’s desire to keep rates low to boost growth.

Advertisement

The challenge for the BoJ, however, is that the comparison rates are also moving. Related Article Opinion

World elections Japan’s election result is a geopolitical earthquake and a ‘very big deal’ for Australia Peter Hartcher Political and international editor The European Central Bank is widely expected to raise its policy rate to 2.5 per cent at its meeting next month. The Fed was under pressure, before last week’s weak jobs data, to hike its rate and the longer the war in the Middle East drags on and seeps into industry costs and the inflation rate, the more probable US rate rises become. Trying to put a floor under the yen carries its own risks, including the potential impact on the carry trade if borrowing costs rise.

Advertisement

Japanese insurers, banks and households are holding trillions of yen in bonds that, because yields on comparable securities have risen, are now worth less than their face value. In the absence of further interventions, Japan’s economic fundamentals – the influences which had driven its currency down – could be expected to reassert themselves. If held to maturity, those unrealised losses are irrelevant, but they do have implications for financial institutions balance sheets – they erode their equity bases – and, in any sale, the losses would become very real. The BoJ will be wary about the potential for a financial crisis if it moves too hard too quickly. What the US intervention signals is the mutual vulnerabilities of the US and Japan and the reality that reducing them, if they can be reduced, won’t be either straightforward, painless or riskless. Japan is confronted with the legacies of nearly 30 years of unconventional policies.

Advertisement

It is trying to navigate an economic transition where it balances systemic and economic stability and the risks of trying to normalise its settings, by growing its way out of the debt and distortions in its economy and financial system that those policies have created. This US administration isn’t given to selfless acts. It isn’t acting, as Trump claimed, out of friendship with Japan. Related Article Opinion

Currencies The real reason Trump just rushed to help Japan Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist It’s doing so because the US is dependent on “Other People’s Money” to fund its government and Americans’ lifestyles. An implosion in the value of the yen is a direct threat to the continued access to that funding, to its economy and financial system and, because of the role the US plays within the global economy and financial system, the rest of the world as well. title: Why Wallabies coach Les Kiss was laughing as Japan Test hung in the balance
text:
Advertisement

Analysis SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Why Wallabies coach Les Kiss was laughing as Japan Test hung in the balance Iain Payten Updated August 10, 2026 — 11:46am ,first published 11:32am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A quick flash of the Australian coaching box in the 68th minute of the Wallabies-Japan clash on Saturday caught an interesting moment: there was Les Kiss, laughing. For context, Australia led 28-25 and were in a real fight. Players were out on their feet, Japan had belief and an historic/disastrous first win by the Brave Blossoms over the Wallabies was very much in the offing. Coach Les Kiss and captain Harry Wilson show their relief after the Wallabies escaped with victory in Japan. Getty Images But if Kiss was feeling the tension, he wasn’t showing it. “It wasn’t a frivolous laugh,” Kiss explained later. “Internally we’re learning about each other in the [coaches] box. At one moment where someone said something, one of the coaches looked at me [and said] is that all right to say that?

Advertisement

“So we’re just seeing how we sit in the coaches box and how we communicate. They’re a good bunch. We’re getting on well.” Kiss did not elaborate, but the laugh came after Declan Meredith put a disappointing night with the boot behind him and kicked deep into a corner after a penalty. Taniela Tupou scored a crucial try soon after. Les Kiss laughing in the Wallabies coaches box during the Japan Test. Stan Sport “It was just a nice little moment where we had a bit of humour in it,” Kiss said. “I know it was tight, but it’s got to be fun doing this too, eh?” In keeping with the “evolution, not revolution” line often rolled out about the Joe Schmidt-Kiss transition, one of the shifts in the new environment seemed to be captured in that light moment.

Advertisement

But that’s not to say Kiss is happy-go-lucky. His opening Test was a pretty stern examination of his coaching – preparation and decision-making during the game. Wallabies players said they felt well prepared for the Osaka oven, having started a heat-acclimatisation plan on day one of camp in Sydney. Kiss noted Japan even had more players than Australia cramping near the end of the game. Isaac Henry and Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii celebrate a tough win. Getty Images And the red card for Miles Amatosero also tested Kiss’ adaptability. Captain Harry Wilson spoke about the clear plan given to the players at half-time to play more narrowly, to conserve energy. The bench rollout was worked well – forwards such as Angus Bell had a strong impact as finishers – and Kiss was not afraid to switch multiple backline positions in the final 20 minutes.

Advertisement

“The intensity is there,” Kiss said about coaching in Test rugby for the first time. “Intense and probably too close to the wire, but yeah, it was good.” Value of a win not always on the stats sheet Eddie Jones wasn’t interested in talking to Japanese media about the Wallabies after the match. Quade Cooper poses for a photograph with a fan in Osaka. Getty Images “I only care about Japan, mate,” he said. “I had my turn to coach Australia.”

Advertisement

But he still inadvertently made a point about the Wallabies’ win when he was questioned about some of his players’ efforts in the loss. “I don’t know what the stats will show, but sometimes there’s more important things than stats,” Jones said. The stats sheet wasn’t overly complimentary about the Wallabies’ performance, but the value of a tick in the only column that counts – win or loss – can’t be underestimated, given the context. Jack Cornelsen palms off Declan Meredith. Getty Images The heat was discussed all week, but it was not a minor thing filling out the news cycle. Tragically, a second division Kyuden Voltex player died last week after being taken to hospital after training on Monday in Fukuoka, reportedly with heatstroke symptoms.

Advertisement

The Test was played at night, but the heat still sapped the players’ energy, and the Wallabies could have wilted. We’ve seen it before: witness Santa Fe in 2024, when Australia lost 67-27 to Argentina. But they didn’t wilt in Osaka and instead ground out an ugly win. It was a hiding to nothing kind of Test for the Wallabies. Japan’s improvement recently hasn’t been digested by most – they beat Italy and also pushed world No. 3 Ireland – and there is still a memory of them from decades ago, and a default expectation Australia should towel them up. It is the same when Australia play Italy and Scotland, and, for some reason, Argentina, too. But the value of a tough win like that, on the road and amid adversity, can be high. The good vibes of a happy shed, and the confidence that comes from consistent wins, can’t be underestimated. The Wallabies haven’t made winning a habit this decade: that was just the fifth time since 2020 they have won two or more Tests in a row.

Advertisement

Japan left kicking themselves With hard-running forwards and a special young talent in Ryunosuke Ito at No.10 – who was plucked out of university rugby and had not played a professional game before his Test debut – Japan were well poised to beat the Wallabies. Loading Jones pointed to fundamental errors as the reason for his side’s loss – 16 in total – but the wisdom of captain Warner Dearns taking a penalty goal in the 50th minute, when Australia still had a player in the sin bin, was baffling. Jeremy Williams was standing on the sideline, ready to enter the fray and return Australia to 15 players. But if Dearns had pushed for a try, he would have had to wait for a stoppage, thus extending the advantage for a few minutes.

Advertisement

Not to mention a try that could have got Japan to 28-26 with half an hour to play. Defensive changes and challenges The one big change the Wallabies spoke about to start the Kiss era was adjusting their defence under former All Blacks defence coach Scott McLeod. Related Article Analysis

Wallabies What Kiss’ approach to attack will mean for million-dollar man Suaalii The conditions and the red card clouded the picture somewhat, but it appeared the Wallabies were looking for much more line speed at set pieces, and a mix of styles in phase attack, holding off to make calls on second-wave plays, but also with a willingness to have a shooter race up. It was mostly a decent first outing, with an 88 per cent effectiveness of the whopping 165 tackles made. But there was also issues to work on near the breakdown, with players switching off and allowing Japan to attack behind it.

title: The alternative to upping interest rates that would leave us with more cash
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

Every time the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) meets to discuss the cash rate, millions of Australians hold their breath, knowing the outcome could affect their mortgage repayments, savings and household budgets.

Some economists say there's another way to cool spending — one that builds your retirement savings instead of handing more money to the bank through higher interest rates.

But it's one almost nobody talks about.

The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) is due to hand down its next cash rate decision on Tuesday. Financial markets and most economists expect the RBA to leave the cash rate unchanged as inflation continues to ease, although the board has indicated it remains focused on returning inflation to its 2 to 3 per cent target.

Cooling inflation means squeezing demand somewhere. While governments can also influence demand through fiscal policy, such as changing taxes or government spending, it's now largely the RBA's job to adjust the cash rate to make borrowing more expensive. Higher interest rates can also strengthen the Australian dollar, making imports cheaper and reducing the demand for exports.
